desc:
Three integer arrays a, b and c are each sorted in non-decreasing order; some of them may be empty but at least one element exists overall. Imagine merging all of them into one sorted array m of length n.

The median of m is m[n / 2] when n is odd, and the average of m[n / 2 - 1] and m[n / 2] when n is even. To avoid fractions, return twice the median, which equals m[(n - 1) / 2] + m[n / 2] using integer division.

a = [1, 4, 9]
b = [2, 3]
c = [5, 6, 7, 8]
merged = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]  (n = 9)
result = 2 * 5 = 10

Merging the arrays costs O(n) time. Aim for something that does not look at every element, such as a time that is logarithmic in the size of the arrays and in the value range.
constraints: 0 ≤ a.length, b.length, c.length ≤ 5,000 and a.length + b.length + c.length ≥ 1
Each array is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: First reduce the task: you need the elements at two positions of the merged order, (n-1)/2 and n/2. How can you find the element at a given position of the merged order without merging?
Binary search on the value: for a candidate value v, the number of elements ≤ v across all arrays is computable with one binary search per array.
The element at 0-based position k of the merged order is the smallest v in [-109, 109] such that at least k + 1 elements are ≤ v. Run this search for k = (n-1)/2 and k = n/2 and add the two answers.
editorial: Let count(v) be the number of elements that are at most v; since every array is sorted it is the sum of three bisect_right calls, each O(log n). The merged element at 0-based position k is the smallest value v with count(v) ≥ k + 1: below it fewer than k + 1 elements fit, and at it the (k+1)-th smallest is covered. count is monotone in v, so a binary search over the value range [-109, 109] finds it in about 31 iterations.

The answer needs the elements at positions (n-1)/2 and n/2 (the same position for odd n, the two middle ones for even n); their sum is twice the median and lies within [-2·109, 2·109], which fits in 32 bits. Total time is O(log V · log n) where V is the value range, and O(1) space. A partition-based search (the classic O(log n) approach for two arrays) generalizes to three arrays, but is considerably harder to get right than this counting search.
